paragraphs.text: This is loose [Liu Bao](liu-bao:definition) from [Cangwu County](cangwu:where-it-is), in the hill country of eastern Guangxi, where the town of Liubao gave the tea its name. Like every [dark tea](dark:definition), the leaf was piled after it was made so that warmth, moisture and microbes could change it, and then it was packed away to age.

It was made in 1980, during the long [decline](cangwu:decline-and-return) that began when war broke the river trade. By the early 1990s very few gardens in the county were still worked. Liu Bao had been made for [Chinese miners and labourers in Southeast Asia](liu-bao:nanyang-trade), and most Liu Bao of this age is [old stock](liu-bao:old-stock) that was left in warehouses in Malaysia and Hong Kong when that trade ended.
At forty-six years it is far past the decade after which Liu Bao counts as [aged](liu-bao:age-aged). For a tea this old, the way it was stored has shaped it as much as the years have.

brewing.text: Liu Bao takes very hot or boiling water, because its leaf is dense and gives up its depth slowly. Rinse it once or twice and pour the rinse away. Use about 5 to 8 grams to 100 ml, start with steeps of five to fifteen seconds and add a few seconds each round; a good Liu Bao gives ten cups or more.

notice.text: A deep red, thick cup with woody, herbal and betel nut notes; tea several decades old is often described with ginseng and camphor.
